newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl hopes recovery can help beat job crisis.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl hopes recovery can help beat job crisis.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Thursday that prospects for economic recovery rested on solid foundations and there was no reason to give up on a government goal of halving unemployment by the turn of the millenium.

Speaking after fresh data showed that unemployment, on a seasonally adjusted basis, hit a post-war record in December of 4.156 million, Kohl said his goal of slashing dole queues would be difficult but not impossible to achieve.
"Fighting unemployment remains the most important domestic policy challenge," he told reporters. "Current levels of over 4.1 million jobless are completely unacceptable."
Kohl said he did not believe that rising unemployment would jeopardise chances of economic recovery this year.
"I think the chances for recovery rest on a solid basis," he said at his traditional New Year news conference. "I see no reason for resignation -- creating jobs is possible."
Underpinning prospects for economic recovery were low interest rates, price stability, a positive global economic outlook and moderate wage settlements, Kohl said.
He also noted that the appreciation of the mark in 1995 had been fully reversed. A weaker mark is seen as helpful to Germany's big export sector.
Kohl also said that a downward revision to its economic forecast by the DIW research institute -- one of six whose forecasts underpin budget policy -- was unfounded.

The Berlin-based DIW -- which has close ties to the Social Democrat (SPD) opposition and trade unions -- predicted this week that gross domestic product would rise by two percent this year. But Kohl said he still supported the view of the six institutes from last autumn of 2.5 percent growth this year.
Preliminary data for 1996 showed on Thursday that the economy grew by a sluggish 1.4 percent.

Discussing negotiations in his three-party, centre-right coalition government on reforming the tax system, Kohl said it was too soon to commit to abolishing the so-called solidarity surcharge, a levy raised to aid rebuilding eastern Germany.
The solidarity surcharge of 7.5 percent on income taxes is due to be cut to 5.5 percent next year.
Fending off demands from the Free Democrats (FDP) for the solidarity charge's abolition by the year 2000, Kohl said that it would be necessary first to finalise a major tax reform plan.
"I cannot make a decision when I don't know what the text of a new tax law will look like," he said.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel's coalition tax commission is due to complete its work on the package of income tax cuts this month, and Kohl said its calculations should also take into account work on reforming the pensions system.
Addressing fears that the greying of the population would make the German pensions system unfinanceable, Kohl said pensions for both young and old would be safe.
Calling for cross-party consensus on pensions reform, Kohl said that the common goal must be to secure pensions for today's 20-, 30- and 40-year-olds.
